site_or_subject: DRC cobalt mine output share, 2025 export ban and quotas
operator: Multiple (CMOC, Glencore, ERG, Gécamines JV); Government of DRC (ARECOMS quotas)
record: USGS records world mined cobalt at 302,000 t (2024) and 310,000 t (2025e), with Congo (Kinshasa) at 226,000 t (2024) and 230,000 t (2025e), an estimated 73% of world total. USGS also records that DRC banned cobalt exports in February 2025, replaced in October 2025 by quotas of 18,125 t for the rest of 2025 and up to 96,600 t/yr for 2026-2027 (incl. 9,600 t strategic reserve); the ARECOMS decision itself was not read.

claim: IISD, an NGO (country profile, June 2026), citing earlier studies, estimates the artisanal (ASM) share at 15-30% of DRC cobalt mine production historically, about 10% of global production in 2020 and about 2% of global production in 2024. Apple's Form SD for calendar 2025 (signed 28 May 2026) covers only tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold; it states 100% of identified 3TG smelters/refiners are required to undergo annual independent third-party audit and that Apple found no reasonable basis to conclude any financed armed groups in the DRC region. Cobalt is not covered by the statutory filing. Mining companies responding to RAID/AFREWATCH (NGOs, 2024) attributed pollution largely to historic contamination and artisanal mining and said their mines run closed circuits; RAID/AFREWATCH say the responses were not accompanied by published third-party audits.

site_or_subject: Copper-mining water demand and desalination shift, 2023-2034
operator: Industry-wide (Codelco, BHP Escondida, Antofagasta Minerals, Collahuasi, others)
record: Cochilco (DEEP 06/2025, June 2025) records total copper-mining water use of 18.8 m3/s (2023) and 18.9 m3/s (2024), projected 22.1 m3/s by 2034. Continental water fell from 12.02 m3/s (63.8%) in 2023 to 10.76 m3/s (56.9%) in 2024 and is projected at 7.6 m3/s in 2034; seawater rose from 6.81 m3/s (36.2%) to 8.16 m3/s (43.1%) and is projected at 14.5 m3/s (about 66%). Cochilco's March 2026 update (DEEP 02/2026) gives total use of 18.5 m3/s in 2024 with 40.7% seawater, and projects 20.6 m3/s in 2034 with 67.6% seawater.

site_or_subject: SQM lithium brine extraction: SMA sanction and compliance program
operator: SQM Salar SpA (Codelco partnership agreed 31 May 2024)
record: Chile's Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente (SMA) opened sanction proceeding Rol F-041-2016 in November 2016 after an audit found brine over-extraction and incomplete information (six infractions [press: Diario Financiero, Minería Chilena]; charge 1 covers brine extraction above the authorised amount between August 2013 and August 2015). The SMA approved SQM Salar's compliance program by Res. Ex. N° 38/2022 of 29 August 2022 (cost more than CLP 46,000 million [press: Diario Financiero], about USD 52 million [press: Reuters via Mining.com]). The program steps the average maximum brine extraction down to 822 L/s from 2027 (slightly under 50% of the limit in RCA 226/2006), a step tied to an EIA still under evaluation, with a limit of 1,026 L/s for the 2025–2026 environmental year, and caps industrial freshwater pumping at 120 L/s (-50% versus RCA 226/2006). SQM filed progress report 15 of 20 on 27 Feb 2026 (program period 30 Aug 2022–28 May 2027). Minería Chilena links the program to the Primer Tribunal Ambiental's ruling in case R-21-2019 [press: Minería Chilena], but that ruling (27 Oct 2020) concerns another procedure: it rejected a claim by the Aymara community of Quillagua and the Quechua community of Huatacondo against SMA Res. Ex. N°24 of 26 Feb 2019, which approved SQM S.A.'s compliance program for the Pampa Hermosa project (Rol D-027-2016, Salar de Llamara), and left that approval in force. Reuters describes the 2022 program as a revision of a previous plan 'mandated by a local environmental court in 2020' [press: Reuters via Mining.com]; no ruling on F-041-2016 was read.

site_or_subject: Indonesian nickel output, captive coal power and concession deforestation
record: USGS records Indonesia nickel mine output of 2,310,000 t (2024) and 2,600,000 t (2025e) of 3,710,000 / 3,900,000 t world (about 62% and 67%, calculated), up an estimated 13% in 2025. A CREA/Global Energy Monitor report (27 Jan 2026) records 19.3 GW of operating captive coal in Indonesia as of July 2025, 15.4 GW of it serving nickel, with 3.6 GW under construction and nearly 31 GW including the announced pipeline [NGO: CREA/GEM]; GEM's Boom and Bust Coal 2025 gave 16.6 GW at end-2024, roughly triple 2019, with 1.1 GW starting construction in 2024 [press: Eco-Business, reporting GEM]. Climate Rights International ('Nickel Unearthed', Jan 2024), using Global Forest Watch data, records at least 5,331 ha of tropical forest cut within Halmahera nickel concessions and at least five captive coal-fired plants built by IWIP [NGO: CRI]. Mongabay's report on the study gives 1,456 ha of forest loss in the Weda Bay Nickel concession as of 2022 [press, source not named: Mongabay; not in the CRI report].

site_or_subject: Heavy rare-earth (ionic clay) mining and exports to China
operator: Unlisted Chinese-linked operators under NDA-K / Kachin Special Region 1 control
record: USGS records Burma rare-earth output of 27,000 t REO (2024) and 22,000 t (2025e), explicitly 'estimated based on reported import data for China'; China's figure is 270,000 t in both years (a production quota excluding undocumented production) of 380,000 t (2024) and 390,000 t (2025e) world (about 70%, calculated). Global Witness (23 May 2024) records more than 300 mining sites in Kachin Special Region 1 by 2023 (+40% since 2021) and expansion in Momauk Township from 9 to over 40 sites, and reports Chinese import data of 41,700 t of heavy rare-earth oxides from Myanmar in 2023 (US$1.4 bn), up from 19,500 t in 2021; its stream sampling showed high acidity and elevated arsenic (no numeric values published) [NGO: Global Witness; the customs data themselves not read]. China imposed export controls on seven REEs in April 2025, expanded them in October 2025, then suspended the October controls for one year in November 2025.

site_or_subject: UN Global E-waste Monitor 2024: generation, formal collection, small IT, transboundary flows
record: GEM 2024 (ITU/UNITAR; launched 20 March 2024; the PDF read is 'Edition 2: November 2024', whose corrigendum (pp. 7-8) does not touch these figures) records 62 billion kg of e-waste generated in 2022 (7.8 kg/capita), of which 13.8 billion kg (22.3%) was documented as formally collected and recycled (pp. 12, 30); Europe 42.8%, Africa under 1% (p. 14); projection 82 billion kg by 2030 with the rate falling to 20% under business as usual (p. 18). Metals value in 2022 e-waste: USD 91 billion (p. 16). Servers are counted within 'professional IT equipment' under large equipment, not as a separate category (p. 108).

site_or_subject: Basel e-waste amendments (in force 1 Jan 2025) vs GPS-tracked and trade-data export flows
record: Decision BC-15/18 (COP-15, 2022) replaced Annex VIII entry A1180 with A1181 (hazardous e-waste) and added Annex II entry Y49 (all other e-waste), making all transboundary e-waste movements subject to prior informed consent from 1 January 2025 for all Parties except those that notified the Depositary of non-acceptance by 1 January 2025. BAN's 'Scam Recycling' (15 Sep 2016) recorded 69 of 205 US-deployed GPS trackers (34%) exported, 37 to Hong Kong, and 23 of 61 recycler-traced exports from R2-certified firms [NGO: BAN]. BAN's EU study (Feb 2019) recorded 19 of 314 devices (6%) exported, 11 (3.5%) to developing countries (Nigeria 5) [NGO: BAN]. BAN's 'Brokers of Shame' (22 Oct 2025) counted 10,026 containers exported by 10 US brokers in 26 months of trade data (Jan 2023–Feb 2025); 8 of 10 brokers were R2V3-certified [NGO: BAN]. A Nexus3 Foundation deck presented at a Basel OEWG-15 side event (25 June 2026) records 914 containers of e-waste from the US at Batam, Indonesia, in 2025-2026 [NGO: Nexus3 Foundation].

site_or_subject: WEEE collection rate vs 65% legal target (Eurostat)
record: Eurostat's Statistics Explained (data from October 2025; PDF generated 28 August 2026) records EEE placed on the market at 14.4 Mt in 2022 and 2023, WEEE collected at 5.2 Mt in 2023 (11.6 kg per inhabitant), and an EU collection rate of 37.5% in 2023 against the 65% target (collected weight relative to average EEE placed on the market in 2020-2022). Bulgaria, Latvia and Slovakia met the 65% (placed-on-market) target and Poland met the alternative 85% target based on WEEE generated; Czechia reached 61.7%. Category 6 'small IT and telecommunication equipment' is defined but no category-level figure is given on the page.

site_or_subject: Used EEE and e-waste imports into Lagos (Person in the Port Project)
operator: UNU-SCYCLE and Basel Convention Coordinating Centre for Africa (BCCC-Africa)
record: The Person in the Port Project (UNU-ViE SCYCLE and BCCC-Africa; container inspections from 23 March 2015; results presented to the Nigerian Government in May 2017; report dated 13 December 2017 in the UNU repository and publicised 27 April 2018) reviewed 3,622 container import documents and inspected 201 containers and 2,184 Ro-Ro vehicles at the Lagos (Apapa) and Tin Can Island ports. site_or_subject: Server/AI hardware depreciation lives in SEC filings vs circularity claims
record: Amazon's SEC filings: servers' useful life 3 to 4 years from 1 Jan 2020, then 4 to 5 years and networking equipment 5 to 6 years from 1 Jan 2022 (Q1-2022 depreciation -USD 973 m; full year 2022 -USD 3.6 bn, with a USD 2.8 bn benefit to net loss), servers 5 to 6 years from 1 Jan 2024 (Q1-2024 -USD 897 m, net income +USD 695 m; full year 2024 -USD 3.2 bn, net income +USD 2.5 bn), then 'a subset of our servers and networking equipment' cut from 6 to 5 years from 1 Jan 2025 due to 'the increased pace of technology development, particularly in the area of artificial intelligence and machine learning' (Q1-2025 depreciation +USD 217 m, net income -USD 162 m, 'primarily impacted our AWS segment'; for the full year 2025 the 10-K gives depreciation +USD 1.4 bn and net income -USD 1.0 bn, or USD 0.10 per share); in Q4 2024 Amazon also retired certain servers and networking equipment early, recording about USD 920 m of accelerated depreciation, for the same stated reason. Alphabet extended servers from 4 to 6 years and certain network equipment from 5 to 6 years beginning FY2023 (Q1-2023 depreciation -USD 988 m, net income +USD 770 m). Microsoft extended server and network equipment from 4 to 6 years beginning FY2023 (Jul-Sep 2022 operating income +USD 1.1 bn). Meta extended most servers and network assets to 5.5 years from 2025 (Q1-2025 depreciation -USD 826 m). Microsoft's 2025 Environmental Data Fact Sheet shows Deloitte & Touche LLP limited assurance on Section 1 (GHG, energy, water and waste tables, with operational waste tonnages and packaging recyclability but no cloud-hardware reuse/recycle percentage) for FY24, with diverted waste of 28,285 t. No public filing stating a physical lifespan for GPUs, or an assured GPU resale/refurbishment volume, was found.
